question: The Commission is continuing to work on further initiatives for the sustainable functioning of data centres, including ratings systems and potential minimum environmental performance standards. However, representatives of the technology sector and infrastructure operators have highlighted major methodological shortcomings and limitations of the database used to prepare these initiatives.
According to the available information, only some of the entities subject to reporting obligations provided the required data, while some Member States are, in practice, not reporting at all.

This raises concerns that the Commission is trying to create far-reaching regulation for strategic digital infrastructure without a sufficient empirical basis, which could negatively affect investment in AI, cloud computing and the development of European technological sovereignty. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission justify continuing to work on potential minimum environmental standards for data centres despite the limited level of data reporting and insufficient representativeness of available information?

How will the Commission ensure that the process of preparing new data centre regulations is based on real operational data and infrastructure operators’ experience rather than primarily on external consultants’ analyses?

Is the Commission considering halting the development of new mandatory standards until more complete and reliable data on the energy and environmental performance of European data centres becomes available?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The European Union is the first to introduce comprehensive legislation on the energy performance and efficiency of data centres. The EU legislative framework, notably the Energy Efficiency Directive1 and its Delegated Act2 increase transparency significantly in this area.

As the report to the European Parliament and the Council on the energy efficiency of data centres in the EU shows that, while data centres in the EU are becoming more sustainable, there is enormous potential for further improvements, especially as part of a better integration with the energy system. The report will be published soon.

Since the Commission is assessing the transposition and implementation of the Energy efficiency Directive, including Article 12 and Annex VII, reporting compliance is expected to improve in next cycles as operators adapt to regulatory requirements and benefit from Commission guidance3.

Furthermore, the Commission supplements reported data with technical studies4,5, stakeholder consultations, including with Member States, and expert validation. Before possibly proposing any minimum performance standards, the Commission will launch a call for evidence and an open public consultation, followed by an impact assessment.

Halting the discussion on possible minimum performance standards when the Commission expects that most of the data centre capacity that will be on the ground in the next 20 years will be designed and be constructed in the next five to seven years, would risk delaying progress toward a sustainable and competitive EU data centre sector.
